title: Stop round-tripping state through map[string]any to compute the delta
description:
The core inefficiency. `mergePatcher.patch` (`go/merge.go:17`) unmarshals every push's full JSON into `map[string]interface{}` and deep-diffs it against the cached previous map. Caching `prev` already avoids the second unmarshal, but the new state is still fully decoded into boxed interfaces every single time — even when one leaf field changed.

## Evidence (rais-main, 342 KB state)

- `json.Unmarshal` into `map[string]any` = **46.8% of process CPU**, **42% of allocated bytes**
- 34,014 allocations per decode, 1.59 MB per decode, 8.4 ms per decode
- median delta actually emitted on the wire: **215 bytes**

So ~342 KB is decoded into ~34k Go objects roughly 3.7x/sec to produce a couple hundred bytes of patch.

## Approaches

1. **Raw-message tree.** Keep `prev` as a lazily-decoded tree of `json.RawMessage` per key. Decode a subtree only when its raw bytes differ from the previous raw bytes — unchanged subtrees collapse to a `bytes.Equal`. Most of a large state is unchanged, so most of the tree is never decoded.
2. **Token-stream diff.** Walk both documents with `encoding/json/jsontext` decoders in lockstep and emit the merge patch directly, never materialising `any`. Zero intermediate boxing, single pass.

Approach 1 is the smaller change and composes with the existing `objectDiff` for the subtrees that do change; approach 2 is the theoretical best. Prototype 1 first and measure against the task-1 benchmark.

## Correctness

Preserve the current RFC 7386 semantics exactly, including deleted keys as `nil`, type-change-forces-replace, and whole-array replacement on any element change (`sliceEqual`). Keep the existing `merge` tests green and add cases for nested add/delete/type-change.
